title: The Wave Equation

blocks.x: A string of length $L$ is fixed at both ends. Let $u(x,t)$ be its displacement. For small vibrations:
Put $u=X(x)T(t)$. Get $X''+\lambda X=0$ and $T'' + c^2\lambda T = 0$.
BCs $X(0)=X(L)=0$ give (Chapter 6) $\lambda_n = (n\pi/L)^2$ and $X_n = \sin\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}$.
With $\omega_n = \dfrac{n\pi c}{L}$, the time equation $T''+\omega_n^2T=0$ gives $T_n = B_n\cos\omega_nt + B_n^*\sin\omega_nt$.
Superpose:
u(x,t) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(B_n\cos\omega_nt + B_n^*\sin\omega_nt\big)\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}.
Use the initial conditions. At $t=0$: $u = \sum B_n\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L} = f(x)$, and $u_t = \sum B_n^*\omega_n\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L} = g(x)$. These are half-range sine series, so
B_n = \frac2L\int_0^L f(x)\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,\dd x, \qquad B_n^* = \frac{2}{n\pi c}\int_0^L g(x)\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,\dd x.

Each term $\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\cos\omega_nt$ is a normal mode. The lowest mode ($n=1$) is the fundamental, with frequency $f_1 = \dfrac{c}{2L}$ Hz. The others (harmonics) have frequencies $nf_1$. This is why a shorter or tighter string gives a higher note.

The mode $n$ has time equation $T'' + c^2\lambda_nT = 0$ with $\lambda_n = (n\pi/L)^2$, so $T'' + \omega_n^2T = 0$ with $\omega_n = c\sqrt{\lambda_n} = \dfrac{n\pi c}{L}$. The solution $T = B\cos\omega_nt + B^*\sin\omega_nt$ oscillates with frequency
f_n = \frac{\omega_n}{2\pi} = \frac{nc}{2L}\ \text{Hz}, \qquad\text{so } f_1 = \frac{c}{2L}\text{ and } f_n = nf_1.
The shape $\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}$ has $n$ half-waves on the string, so its wavelength is $2L/n$. With $c = \sqrt{T/\rho}$ we see why the pitch rises when the string is shorter or tighter.
B_n = \frac2\pi\int_0^\pi x(\pi-x)\sin nx\,\dd x.

Integrate by parts twice: $\displaystyle\int_0^\pi x(\pi-x)\sin nx\,\dd x = \frac{2\big(1-(-1)^n\big)}{n^3}$. So $B_n = \dfrac{4(1-(-1)^n)}{\pi n^3}$, which is $\dfrac{8}{\pi n^3}$ for odd $n$ and $0$ for even $n$.
u(x,t) = \frac8\pi\sum_{n\ \text{odd}}\frac{\sin nx\cos nt}{n^3}.
The terms fall as $1/n^3$, so only the first few modes matter. Check at $t=0$, $x=\pi/2$: $\frac8\pi\big(1 - \frac1{27} + \frac1{125} - \cdots\big)\approx 2.467$, and $f(\pi/2) = \pi^2/4 = 2.467$. ✓

$L=\pi$, $c=1$, $f=0$, $g(x) = \sin 2x$. All $B_n=0$. $B_n^* = \dfrac{2}{n\pi}\displaystyle\int_0^\pi\sin 2x\sin nx\,\dd x$. By orthogonality this is zero unless $n=2$, and for $n=2$ it equals $\dfrac{2}{2\pi}\cdot\dfrac\pi2 = \dfrac12$. So
u(x,t) = \tfrac12\sin 2x\,\sin 2t.
Check: $u_t(x,0) = \sin 2x$. ✓
For a very long string, with no ends, we do not need Fourier series.
For $u_{tt} = c^2u_{xx}$ on $-\infty<x<\infty$ with $u(x,0)=f(x)$ and $u_t(x,0)=g(x)$:
u(x,t) = \frac12\big[f(x-ct) + f(x+ct)\big] + \frac{1}{2c}\int_{x-ct}^{x+ct}g(s)\,\dd s.
Step 1: new variables. Let $\xi = x - ct$ and $\eta = x + ct$, and write $u(x,t) = U(\xi,\eta)$. By the chain rule, $\xi_x = \eta_x = 1$, $\xi_t = -c$, $\eta_t = c$:
u_x = U_\xi + U_\eta,\qquad u_t = -cU_\xi + cU_\eta.
Apply the same rules again:
u_{xx} = U_{\xi\xi} + 2U_{\xi\eta} + U_{\eta\eta},\qquad u_{tt} = c^2\big(U_{\xi\xi} - 2U_{\xi\eta} + U_{\eta\eta}\big).
So $u_{tt} - c^2u_{xx} = -4c^2U_{\xi\eta}$, and the wave equation becomes $U_{\xi\eta} = 0$.
Step 2: solve. $U_{\xi\eta} = 0$ means $U_\xi$ does not depend on $\eta$, so $U_\xi = \varphi'(\xi)$ and $U = \varphi(\xi) + \psi(\eta)$. Therefore
u(x,t) = \varphi(x - ct) + \psi(x + ct).

Step 3: initial conditions. At $t=0$: $\varphi(x) + \psi(x) = f(x)$ and $u_t(x,0) = -c\varphi'(x) + c\psi'(x) = g(x)$. Integrate the second one: $\psi(x) - \varphi(x) = \frac1c\int_{x_0}^xg(s)\,\dd s + K$. Solving the two equations,
\varphi(x) = \frac12f(x) - \frac1{2c}\int_{x_0}^xg\,\dd s - \frac K2,\qquad \psi(x) = \frac12f(x) + \frac1{2c}\int_{x_0}^xg\,\dd s + \frac K2.
Put $x - ct$ into $\varphi$ and $x+ct$ into $\psi$ and add. The constants $K$ and $x_0$ cancel, and we get
u(x,t) = \frac12\big[f(x-ct) + f(x+ct)\big] + \frac1{2c}\int_{x-ct}^{x+ct}g(s)\,\dd s.

Meaning. The term $f(x-ct)$ is the shape $f$ moving to the right with speed $c$. The term $f(x+ct)$ moves to the left. An initial bump with zero velocity splits into two bumps of half the height that travel apart. In general every solution has the form $\varphi(x-ct) + \psi(x+ct)$.
$f(x)=\sin x$, $g=0$: $u = \tfrac12[\sin(x-ct) + \sin(x+ct)] = \sin x\cos ct$. This is the standing wave from Chapter 9, problem 5. ✓
A string with $L=\pi$, $c=1$ starts with $u(x,0) = \sin x - 3\sin 2x$ and $u_t(x,0)=0$. Find $u(x,t)$.
A string with $L=\pi$, $c=2$ has $f=0$ and $g(x) = \sin x$. Find $u(x,t)$.
Find the fundamental frequency of a string with $L=0.65$ m and wave speed $c=300$ m/s.
Use d’Alembert’s formula with $f(x) = \sin x$, $g=0$.
For $L = \pi$, $c=1$, $g=0$, $f(x)=x(\pi - x)$, write the first two non-zero terms of $u(x,t)$.

(1) $B_1=1$, $B_2=-3$: $u = \sin x\cos t - 3\sin 2x\cos 2t$.   (2) $\omega_1 = \pi c/L = 2$, $B_1^* = \dfrac{2}{\pi\cdot 2}\displaystyle\int_0^\pi\sin^2x\,\dd x = \dfrac12$: $u = \tfrac12\sin x\sin 2t$.   (3) $f_1 = c/(2L) = 300/1.3 \approx 231$ Hz.   (4) $u = \sin x\cos ct$.   (5) $u\approx\dfrac8\pi\Big(\sin x\cos t + \dfrac{\sin 3x\cos 3t}{27}\Big)$.
